```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)      # For scale_color_colorblind()
library(palmerpenguins) # For penguins dataset
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title = "Body mass and flipper length",
    subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)",
    color = "Species", shape = "Species"
  ) +
  scale_color_colorblind()

```

```{r}
# 3
# Scatterplot of species vs. bill_depth_mm
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = species, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point()
#boxplot
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = species, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Depth by Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)"
  )
# conclusion A scatterplot is not suitable for a categorical variable like species. A better choice is a boxplot.

```

```{r}
# 1.43
#1
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(y = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Count of Penguin Species",
    x = "Count",
    y = "Species"
  )
#Mapping species to the y-axis makes the bars horizontal instead of vertical, with the count shown on the x-axis.


```

```{r}
# 1.43
#2
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(color = "red")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "red")
#The first plot colors only the bar outlines, while the second fills the bars; fill is more useful for changing bar colors.
```

```{r}
# 1.43
#3
#The bins argument in geom_histogram() controls the number of bins used to divide the data range, affecting the granularity of the histogram.
```

```{r}
# 1.43
#4
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Diamond Carat Weights",
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Count"
  )
#experementing with other bin
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Histogram with Binwidth = 0.01",
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Count"
  )
#The histogram reveals sharp peaks and gaps, showing fine details in distribution and highlighting popular carat sizes like 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 carats.

```

```{r}
# 1.5
# 1. Exploring mpg dataset: Categorical vs. Numerical Variables
?mpg
# View structure of the mpg dataset
str(mpg)
# Get a summary to distinguish categorical and numerical variables
summary(mpg)

```

```{r}
#1.5
# 2. Scatterplot of hwy vs. displ
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  )
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement (Colored by City MPG)",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "City MPG"
  )

# Mapping a third numerical variable to size
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = cty)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement (Sized by City MPG)",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    size = "City MPG"
  )

# Mapping to both color and size
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty, size = cty)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement (Color & Size by City MPG)",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "City MPG",
    size = "City MPG"
  )

# Mapping to shape (Only works for categorical variables)
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG vs. Engine Displacement (Shape by Drive Type)",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    shape = "Drive Type"
  )


```

```{r}
#1.5
# 3. Mapping a third variable to linewidth
ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, linewidth = cty)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of Mapping to Linewidth",
    x = "Engine Displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    linewidth = "City MPG"
  )
# Observation: linewidth doesn't apply well to points and works better for lines.


```

```{r}
#1.5
# 5. Scatterplot of bill_depth_mm vs. bill_length_mm (Colored by species)
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Depth vs. Bill Length (Colored by Species)",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    color = "Species"
  )
# Faceting by species
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Depth vs. Bill Length (Faceted by Species)",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)"
  )
# Observation: Coloring shows species-specific clustering, while faceting separates species entirely.


```

```{r}
#1.5
# 6. Why does the following yield two separate legends?
ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(color = "Species")

# Fix: Use labs() to set both color and shape together
ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Dimensions with Combined Legend",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    color = "Species",
    shape = "Species"
  )
# Observation: Legends are combined when the same label is used for both aesthetics.



```

```{r}
#1.5
# 7. Stacked Bar Plots for Species & Island
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Penguin Species by Island",
    x = "Island",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Species"
  )
# Question Answered: What proportion of each species lives on each island?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Islands for Each Penguin Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Island"
  )
# Question Answered: What proportion of each species is found on each island?

```

```{r}
# 1.6
#  Create a bar plot
bar_plot <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar()

#  Create a scatterplot
scatter_plot <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()

# . Display both plots (last one shown is saved by default)
bar_plot
scatter_plot

# 4. Save the last created plot (scatter plot) as PNG
ggsave("mpg-plot.png")  # This saves the scatter plot because it was last created

# 5. To save the bar plot instead, explicitly specify the plot
ggsave("mpg-bar-plot.png", plot = bar_plot)

# 6. Save the plot as a PDF instead of PNG
ggsave("mpg-plot.pdf")

# 7. Find out what file formats are supported
?ggsave  # Opens the documentation for ggsave()

```
